newsitem.title: USA: Doctors still debate whether implants cause disease.
newsitem.headline: Doctors still debate whether implants cause disease.

text.p: By Maggie Fox, Health Correspondent
Women suing Dow Chemical Co say it is clear silicone breast implants have made them ill, but scientists studying the safety of silicones say evidence is still scanty and conflicting.

A Louisiana jury ruled on Monday that Dow Chemical was negligent in testing silicone for use in human implants and intentionally withheld information, but has not decided whether the implants actually cause disease.
That stage of the trial begins on Sept. 29.
Dow argues there is little evidence the implants can make people ill. "Breast implants do not cause harm," Dow Chemical lead attorney Lorna Propes said after Monday's decision.

The women who are suing complain of illnesses including rheumatoid arthritis; lupus, which has symptoms ranging from skin lesions to kidney failure, and scleroderma, marked by deposits of connective tissue in the skin.
Such autoimmune disorders arise when the body's defenses mistakenly turn inwards.

The U.S. government has taken a cautious approach towards the use of silicone implants. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA), which regulates drugs and devices such as implants, withdrew approval of silicone gel implants in 1992 except for women in breast cancer trials.
"It is unclear at this time whether the signs and symptoms experienced by these women are related to their implants," the FDA says in its latest information booklet on breast implants.
Most studies looking at large populations find no increased risk of autoimmune disease among women with implants -- or just a very small increase in risk.
The main concern is the possibility that small amounts of silicone can leak out of the implants even if there is no rupture.
Although it was believed silicone was inert and would not cause a reaction in the body, some recent studies indicate the immune system does sometimes respond to the compound.

Several studies published in the Journal of Autoimmunity have found that some women with the silicone implants have antibodies to their own collagen -- an important protein component of connective tissue.
Earlier this year researchers at Louisiana's Tulane University found antibodies to unidentified polymers in women with implants.
Silicone gel itself is made up of many different polymers.
Mike Potter, a researcher at the National Cancer Institute, said he had found a possible biological basis for some silicone polymers to cause such a reponse.
Working with mice genetically bred to grow tumours, he found that while most silicones were inert, others caused little bodies known as granulomas to grow in the mice.
"The length of these polymers is apparently important," Potter said in a telephone interview.
The gel is made up of a mixture of long and short polymers. The shorter polymers are more liquid.
But they may also be small enough to be absorbed by immune system cells known as macrophages, Potter said.

"Maybe the macrophage can ingest it and maybe this causes havoc with the membranes inside the macrophage," he said. Macrophages, when in distress, often release cytokines -- signaling chemicals that can cause an inflammatory response.
Potter stressed that his work was still very preliminary. He also said not all people would react to the chemicals.
"People react genetically in a different way to the implants. Some people have a very low reactivity ... and others form a more inflammatory reaction," he said.
